Getting started with meridianR

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

meridianR is an R interface to Google Meridian, a Bayesian Marketing Mix Modeling (MMM) library. It wraps the Meridian Python package with reticulate, pairing faithful bindings to Meridian’s objects with an idiomatic R layer.

Installation

Meridian runs on Python (JAX or TensorFlow, with TensorFlow Probability). Install it once into a persistent r-meridian environment:

meridianR::install_meridian()

This installs the newest tested Meridian release (2.2.1); any release from 1.7.1 to 2.2.1 can be chosen with meridian_version. If no Python 3.11–3.13 is available, one is installed first. Use install_meridian(gpu = TRUE) for the CUDA build. If you skip this step, meridianR still works: reticulate provisions an environment automatically the first time you use a Meridian function.

In each new session, bind that environment before anything else touches Python, then load the package:

reticulate::use_virtualenv("r-meridian", required = TRUE)
library(meridianR)
meridian_version()

meridianR uses Meridian’s default compute backend: JAX from Meridian 2.2 (where TensorFlow is deprecated), TensorFlow before that. Call use_backend("tensorflow") or use_backend("jax") before first use to choose one explicitly.

Assemble input data

Meridian expects long-format data: one row per geo-by-time, with columns for the KPI, population, media spend, and any controls. as_meridian_input() turns such a data frame into a Meridian InputData object.

data("sales")

input <- as_meridian_input(
  sales,
  kpi            = "conversions",
  time           = "week",
  geo            = "region",
  population     = "population",
  media_spend    = c("tv_spend", "search_spend"),
  media          = c("tv_impressions", "search_clicks"),
  media_channels = c("TV", "Search"),
  controls       = "price_index"
)
input

If you only have spend (no impressions), omit media and spend is used as the media metric. For a national (single-geo) model, pass national = TRUE.

For step-by-step control, use the fluent builder instead:

input <- input_data_builder("non_revenue", geo = "region", time = "week") |>
  with_kpi(sales, kpi_col = "conversions") |>
  with_population(sales) |>
  with_media(sales,
    media_cols       = c("tv_impressions", "search_clicks"),
    media_spend_cols = c("tv_spend", "search_spend"),
    media_channels   = c("TV", "Search")) |>
  build_input_data()

Configure priors and the model specification

model_spec() controls the adstock/lag, saturation, and priors. Meridian’s defaults are well chosen, so a minimal spec is often all you need:

spec <- model_spec(max_lag = 8, media_effects_dist = "log_normal")
spec

Priors and KPI scale. conversions is a non-revenue KPI and we did not supply revenue_per_kpi, so Meridian places a prior on each channel’s total media contribution by default – no per-channel calibration needed. You can override priors with prior_distribution() and the prior_*() constructors, but they must match your KPI’s scale. In particular, an ROI prior such as prior_lognormal(0.2, 0.9) (median ROI ~ 1.2) describes a revenue KPI, where ROI is dollars per dollar. For a conversions KPI, ROI is conversions per dollar – typically far below 1 – so that prior would be off by orders of magnitude and massively over-credit media. Either keep the default, supply revenue_per_kpi so ROI is dollar-based, or customize a scale-free prior such as the adstock decay rate alpha_m (which always lives on [0, 1]):

model_spec(
  max_lag = 8,
  prior   = prior_distribution(alpha_m = prior_beta(3, 3))
)

For a non-revenue KPI, the most natural informative prior is usually on each channel’s share of the KPI. Switch the prior family with media_prior_type and supply contribution_m (one value per channel, in channel order):

model_spec(
  max_lag          = 8,
  media_prior_type = "contribution",
  prior            = prior_distribution(contribution_m = prior_beta(c(3, 2), c(20, 30)))
)

The other choices are "roi" (the default, roi_m), "mroi" (mroi_m), and "coefficient" (beta_m). Adstock is controlled by max_lag, the adstock_decay_spec ("geometric" or "binomial", or a named list per channel), and the alpha_m prior.

Baseline knots. For a geo model, Meridian’s default is one baseline knot per time period (104 here), which is very flexible and can converge slowly. A smaller number, e.g. model_spec(knots = 10), or automatic knot selection with model_spec(enable_aks = TRUE) often fits faster and mixes better. Check rhat_summary() after fitting.

Fit the model

Create the model, then draw from the prior and posterior. fit() does both:

mmm <- meridian_model(input, spec)

fit(mmm, n_chains = 7, n_adapt = 500, n_burnin = 500, n_keep = 1000)

mmm
summary(mmm)

Sampling modifies the model in place (draws are stored on the model’s ArviZ inference_data), so sample_prior(), sample_posterior(), and fit() all return the same model object.

Save and reload 

save_model(mmm, "mmm.binpb")
mmm <- load_model("mmm.binpb")

The .binpb extension selects Meridian’s versioned schema format, which other Meridian versions can read. A .pkl path uses the legacy pickle format instead; it only reloads under the same Meridian version and is deprecated from Meridian 2.2.

Drop down to Python

Everything in Meridian is reachable through the meridian module handle, the low-level escape hatch beneath the wrappers:

meridian$analysis$analyzer$Analyzer(mmm)

For tidy metrics, diagnostics, and ggplot2 charts of a fitted model, see vignette("analysis").
